name: Burnt-matchstick lash darkener

lead: Before commercial mascara was widely sold, people darkened lashes and brows with homemade mixtures based on soot, ash or charcoal. The burnt-matchstick version uses the blackened tip of a spent match as a ready-made pigment. The visual payoff is the same as mascara: darker, more defined lashes that make the eyes look larger and framed.

The broader tradition is documented: kohl in ancient Egypt, and Victorian mixtures of ash or lampblack with elderberry juice. Specific accounts of matchsticks are folk-practice descriptions, and no clinical research has examined them.

paras: Accounts describe rubbing the cooled, charred tip along the lash line or brow. Modern users who try it as a retro or no-product trick describe it as smudge-prone and removable with ordinary cleanser.

Soot and ash are not made or tested for use on the eye area. Contact with the eye can irritate it, and cosmetics regulators in the US have regulated eye-area products since the 1930s after severe injuries from a permanent lash dye.

angle.text: The soot works as a dark pigment applied to lashes, giving a defined look similar to mascara. It is a temporary cosmetic effect that wipes off.

lead: Darkening the lashes and brows with burnt material is an old beauty technique that predates commercial mascara. The burnt-matchstick variant uses the carbonized head of a spent match as a pigment, a household substitute for cosmetic color. It makes lashes look darker and thicker at the root and frames the eyes [1].

The wider history is documented. Kohl, made from minerals, charcoal or soot, darkened lashes and lids from about 4000 BC in ancient Egypt, and Victorian women reportedly heated ash or lampblack with elderberry juice for lashes [1]. Commercial mascara followed with Rimmel and, in 1915, Thomas Lyle Williams's product that became Maybelline [1].
No published study has examined burnt matchsticks as a cosmetic.

paras: Lash darkening with soot-based kohl is recorded from roughly 4000 BC in ancient Egypt and continued through Babylonian, Greek and Roman cultures; it faded in Europe after Rome but remained common in the Middle East [1]. Victorian women made lash color from ash or lampblack with elderberry juice [1].
Eugene Rimmel's petroleum-jelly-based cosmetic gave "rimmel" its meaning as mascara in several languages, and Williams's 1915 product led to Maybelline in 1917 [1].

A permanent lash dye containing para-phenylenediamine, Lash Lure, blinded a number of women in the 1930s, and Congress gave the FDA authority to regulate cosmetics in 1938 [1]. Eye-area products are therefore regulated, while soot and ash are not manufactured or tested as cosmetics.
